title: Quantum Fidelity-per-Cost: A Metric for Evaluation of Quantum Computing Systems
abstract: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made hardware comparison not only a physics benchmark but also a practical purchasing decision. Cost-aware comparison of quantum computers remains underexplored and is difficult to do under the heterogeneous billing models offered by various cloud-based quantum computing providers. This paper makes two main contributions to enable price-aware comparison of quantum computers. First, this work presents a cross-provider measurement study of quantum circuit execution fidelity spanning 14 cloud QPU access-path entries (12 distinct physical QPUs) across four cloud access paths: Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud, IBM Quantum Runtime (IBM) cloud, IQM Resonance (IQM) cloud, and Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) cloud. Second, this work proposes and analyzes a cost-aware score, Quantum Fidelity-per-Cost (QFC), which combines Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence from an ideal output distribution, shot count, and monetary cost into one possible metric under a documented billing model. The main empirical observation from this work is that cost-aware ranking can differ from purely fidelity-based evaluation of quantum computers, and that users may select different quantum computing backends when they consider price in their selection, as opposed to selection based on fidelity alone. This work shows that the ranking is stable under reweighting of the metric, and that a device's billing model, not its hardware, governs how its score scales with shot count. Reported QFC values change as new machines come online or as providers revise their prices.
summary: This paper introduces Quantum Fidelity-per-Cost (QFC), a novel metric designed to compare cloud quantum computers by integrating execution fidelity with the actual monetary cost. Through extensive cross-provider measurements, the authors demonstrate that considering price leads to different hardware rankings than focusing solely on physical performance metrics like fidelity. This provides a necessary framework for practical, real-world adoption of quantum computing resources.
main_problem: The authors address the difficulty of comparing quantum computing hardware accessed via cloud services due to heterogeneous and complex billing models.
main_result: A cost-aware metric, Quantum Fidelity-per-Cost (QFC), was proposed, showing that ranking based on price can significantly differ from rankings based purely on fidelity.
method: The study involves a cross-provider measurement of quantum circuit execution fidelity across multiple cloud QPUs and combines this with monetary cost into the QFC score.
model_or_system: The platform consists of superconducting qubits accessed through four major cloud providers (AWS, IBM Quantum, IQM Resonance, OQC), tested using a narrow two-qubit Bell-state workload.
key_observables: Quantum Fidelity (measured via KL divergence and TVD), monetary cost ($C$), and the derived QFC score.
important_parameters: Shot count ($N$), billing model parameters ($c_{	ext{task}}, c_{	ext{shot}}, c_{	ext{sec}}$), and sensitivity weighting factors ($\alpha,  eta, \gamma$).
main_assumptions: The metric is workload-specific (Bell state) and dependent on a snapshot of provider pricing; the comparison assumes defined billing models apply consistently.
figures_summary: Figures compare mean TVD vs. shots, show QFC vs. shot count for different billing models, and illustrate that fidelity-based ordering differs from QFC ordering.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of cost-aware benchmarking, details the cross-provider measurement study using a specific workload, proposes and analyzes the QFC metric, presents empirical results comparing fidelity vs. cost rankings, and discusses stability analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on cloud infrastructure, the development of rigorous, quantifiable metrics for performance evaluation (like QFC) is crucial for any field relying on complex quantum hardware access, including those simulating open quantum systems or requiring resource estimation.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Bell-state fidelity error. Mean TVD falls with shot count on every provider, but the ordering of devices is largely fixed by 100 shots; at 1000 shots the spread across access paths is a factor of five, from 0.025 (IBM Marrakesh) to 0.130 (IBM Torino, retired). Color encodes provider; IQM entries are annotated with the cloud they were reached through.

Fig. 2. The 1000-shot ordering by fidelity (left) against the ordering by QFC (right). Every crossing line is an access path whose standing changes once price is accounted for. The two emphasized lines are the largest movers: trapped-ion IonQ Aria-1 has the best fidelity in the study but falls to 14th by value, while IQM Sirius rises from 9th to 1st.

Fig. 3. QFC vs. shot count on log–log axes (α = β = γ = 1). Thin lines are individual access paths, colored by billing model; bold lines are the median of each group. The three models produce three distinct shapes: per-shot-only billing is flat in N, task-plus-shot billing rises and saturates, and runtime billing rises with unit slope because the billed duration barely depends on N.
